rv.q: Written by David Lindsay-Abaire with a keen understanding of human nature and directed by Kenny Leon with a master’s skill for building onstage drama to a fever pitch, “The Balusters,” which debuts tonight at Manhattan Theatre Club, may be the most vital and timely show on Broadway t...
The Balusters feels more like the latter – which makes it both more fun and less resonant than it probably should be.
The Balusters ultimately doesn't have enough thematic heft to feel like much more than an entertaining diversion.
Top-notch comedy and covetable home decor—all in a tidy 100-minute package.
David Lindsay-Abaire's fresh and funny comedy uses the pettiness, blind spots and outright biases of the diverse characters who are involved to comment with sharp insight on The Way We Live Now.

The Neighborhood Association is meeting this week in the gorgeous, newly renovated home of neighborhood newcomer Kyra (Anika Noni Rose), a Black doctor (race is not mentioned here casually; stay tuned), who is eager to get involved in her new surroundings and just as eager to forget what happened at her old surroundings.
The Ballusters provides more gut-busting laughter than any show this season.
It doesn't seek to push the genre into bold, modern directions but to embrace the virtues of a well-constructed contemporary satire.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).

Headout and SeatPlan both flag rows E-J as the best price-to-sightline ratio: meaningfully cheaper than the A-D premium band while staying close in a 634-seat room. Slight orchestra rake keeps sightlines clean. Mezzanine overhang (per SeatPlan) begins at row G but the intimate room means no sound-deadening issue in this band.
